title: Why Do So Many Celebrity Pastors Fall? Power and Platform
subtitle: Celebrity pastor culture, the abuse of spiritual authority, and why so many famous leaders fall
question: Why do the men we built into giants keep collapsing, and what did we want from them that no man was ever meant to carry?
whyItMatters:
A platform is not a sin. A pedestal is a different thing, and the church has lost the ability to tell them apart. We took men gifted to preach and we made them brands. We took the weight of a calling and we hung it on a personality. Then we acted surprised when the personality could not bear the weight, when the marriage cracked, when the staff testified, when the pattern that everyone near the throne already knew finally reached the rest of us. The fall of a famous leader is treated as a scandal, a single man's secret undone. It is rarely that. It is a system doing exactly what it was built to do.

I write this with a platform of my own. I have a website with my name on it, books with my face on the back, a network of pastors who read what I publish. That is the honest place to start. The temptation I am describing is not a temptation I observe from outside. It is one I am inside of every time I check whether the thing I wrote was shared. The question is not whether a man has influence. The question is what the influence is doing to him, and whether anyone in his life still has the standing to tell him no.
biblicalFoundation:
Jesus settles the matter before the church ever has the chance to confuse it. The disciples are arguing about greatness, jockeying for the seats on the right and the left, and he does not soften it. The rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, he says, and their great ones exercise authority over them. Then the hinge of the whole Christian understanding of power. It shall not be so among you. Whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first must be slave of all. The world's pyramid is turned over. The one at the top is the one underneath, holding the weight, washing the feet. Every pastor who has read this and still built a kingdom has read past the verse that condemns him.

Peter, who knew something about wanting to be first, writes to elders with the scar tissue of a man who learned the hard way. Shepherd the flock of God that is among you, he says, not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock. The shepherd leads by being the kind of man the sheep can safely follow, not by standing over them with a rod. Authority in the New Testament is downward pressure absorbed, not upward power claimed. The moment a leader uses the flock instead of feeding it, he has stopped being a shepherd and become the thing Ezekiel names.

And Ezekiel names it without mercy. Woe to the shepherds of Israel who have been feeding themselves. Should not shepherds feed the sheep? You eat the fat, you clothe yourselves with the wool, you slaughter the fat ones, but you do not feed the sheep. The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the strays you have not sought. With force and harshness you have ruled them. This is the celebrity machine described twenty-six centuries early. The flock exists to feed the shepherd's appetite, to fund the building, to fill the seats, to grow the number that proves the man's importance. Jesus raises the stakes higher than any of us want to sit with. Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him to have a great millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depth of the sea. The men who used their platforms to wound the vulnerable did not commit a small sin. They earned the worst sentence Jesus ever pronounced.

John gives us the smallest and most familiar portrait of all. There was a man named Diotrephes, he writes, who likes to put himself first. He does not acknowledge our authority, he refuses to welcome the brothers, he stops those who want to and puts them out of the church. No heresy is listed. No doctrine is named. His sin is simply that he loved to be first, and a church organized around a man who loves to be first will always, in the end, expel anyone who threatens his place. Empire does not require false teaching. It only requires a throne and a man who will not leave it.

churchRecord.led: The church has, at its best, produced the opposite of the celebrity pastor. It produced the desert fathers who fled acclaim into the silence. It produced a Bonhoeffer who walked back into Germany toward a scaffold rather than keep his reputation safe in New York. It produced ten thousand unnamed pastors who buried the poor, sat with the dying, and preached to forty people for forty years without a book deal. The servant model is not a theory the church invented and abandoned. It is a life the church has lived, quietly, in every generation that the cameras never found.
churchRecord.failed: And the church has also built the machine. We platformed men we knew were unwell because they filled the room. We signed the books, sold the conference tickets, and looked away from the staff who left broken. We confused the gift of speech with the character of holiness, as if a man who could move a crowd must therefore be safe to follow into the dark. When the falls came, we performed shock we had not earned, because the warning signs had been visible to everyone close enough to see, and proximity to a famous man had been made too valuable to risk by telling the truth.

whereWeAgree: Almost everyone, believer or not, can see that authority exists for the sake of the people under it, and that authority without accountability is the most dangerous arrangement human beings have ever devised. The watching world is not wrong to recoil at the fallen pastor. It is reading the gospel back to us more accurately than we read it to ourselves.
captureLeft: The progressive instinct names the abuse of the powerful clearly, and then builds its own pedestals out of different material. Influence culture, the activist with the brand, the thought leader whose platform becomes its own unaccountable kingdom, the deplatforming that simply relocates the throne. The left critiques hierarchy while constructing a status ladder of its own, measured in followers and moral standing rather than in stained glass.
captureRight: The conservative church has too often baptized the entrepreneur and called him a prophet, treating the megachurch as a brand to be scaled and the pastor as a founder whose vision must not be questioned. It mistook market success for divine favor, growth for faithfulness, and the absence of accountability for the freedom of the anointed. The bigger the platform grew, the fewer the people permitted to speak into it.

right.label: The celebrity megachurch and the unaccountable pastor
right.whatItLooksLike: A church built around one charismatic founder whose name is the brand and whose vision is treated as beyond question. Governance is structured so that the senior leader cannot easily be removed, elders are often loyalists, and growth in attendance and reach is read as the proof of God's favor. The platform expands faster than the character or the accountability meant to hold it.
right.inThePast: The model has deep American roots. Early radio and television preachers like Aimee Semple McPherson and later Billy Graham showed how mass media could turn a single voice into a national figure. The 1980s televangelist collapse made the pattern public, with the Jim Bakker financial fraud conviction and the Jimmy Swaggart prostitution scandal exposing how little accountability sat under enormous reach. Each fall was reported as a personal failing rather than a structural one.
right.now: Mainstream reporting has documented a long sequence of fallen celebrity leaders. Mark Driscoll resigned from Mars Hill in 2014 amid plagiarism and bullying findings, a story examined in the Christianity Today podcast The Rise and Fall of Mars Hill. Bill Hybels left Willow Creek in 2018 after multiple women reported misconduct, and a posthumous report on Ravi Zacharias in 2021 confirmed credible allegations of abuse. Carl Lentz was dismissed from Hillsong in 2020, after which further reporting and the documentary series on Hillsong widened the picture.
named: the church growth and megachurch model

left.label: The progressive thought leader and the deconstruction influencer
left.whatItLooksLike: A teaching authority that no church ordained and no body can revoke, conferred instead by an audience and an algorithm. The online teacher gathers a following through podcasts, books, and social feeds, and the relationship is parasocial, intimate in feeling yet one directional in fact. Standing is measured in followers and reach, and correction is hard to deliver because the audience belongs to the individual rather than to any congregation.
left.inThePast: Religious teaching outside formal ordination is not new. The mass paperback and the conference stage already let figures like Rachel Held Evans reach readers far beyond any local church, and the wider deconstruction conversation grew through blogs and book tours in the 2000s and 2010s. The self help and personal brand tradition, traced by writers on American religion back through figures like Norman Vincent Peale, long blurred the line between author and pastor, between platform and pulpit.
left.now: The creator and influencer economy has become its own engine of religious authority. Platforms reward confident, frequent, emotionally direct content, and the result is teaching offices built entirely on reach, with figures such as Glennon Doyle building large followings around personal narrative and moral guidance. Documented features of this economy include parasocial attachment, monetization through Patreon, Substack, and merchandise, and the deplatforming dynamic that removes a voice from one site only to relocate it to another. The throne moves but it does not disappear.
named: Rachel Held Evans and the progressive blogosphere
Glennon Doyle and personal narrative platforms
the self help and personal brand tradition

whereWeDiffer: The gospel does not ask us to tear down every platform or pretend influence can be erased. It asks something harder. That a man with a platform stay genuinely accountable to people who can remove him, that he treat his fame as a danger to be managed rather than a reward to be enjoyed, and that he measure his ministry by the health of the weakest sheep rather than the size of the strongest crowd.
theCost: To say this honestly is to indict the system that pays many of us. The conference circuit, the book economy, the algorithm that rewards the confident and buries the careful, all of it runs on the engine of the platform, and the man who names the engine is biting the hand that feeds his name. There is a cost to refusing the pedestal even when the platform remains. It means building accountability that can actually hurt you, submitting to people who can say no and make it stick, and being willing to grow smaller so that the flock can grow safer. Most of us would rather keep the applause and grieve the fallen from a distance.
charge: Look at the leaders you have made large, and ask who in their life is still permitted to tell them the truth. Then turn the question on yourself, on the influence you have however small, on the room where you are the loudest voice, and find the person who can correct you and refuse to remove them. The pedestal does not fall on its own. It is dismantled, one act of submission at a time, by people who decided that being a servant was not a stage they passed through on the way to greatness. It was the greatness. It was always the only greatness there was.
